items.stem: A service lift is descending but its downward speed is decreasing. Taking upward as positive, what direction must its net force point?

options.A: Upward, since its acceleration opposes its downward velocity.
options.B: Downward, because it is moving downward.
options.C: Zero, because the slowing is steady.
options.D: The direction cannot be inferred without its mass.

scaffolds.author: NLM-PROD1
scaffolds.text: Name the direction of travel, what happens to speed, and which force quantity is being asked for. Does travel direction alone decide net-force direction?

scaffolds.author: NLM-PROD1
scaffolds.text: Treat a downward velocity as a negative number. Compare an earlier and later velocity when the downward speed is shrinking. Which value is closer to zero, and what does their change per second mean?

scaffolds.author: NLM-PROD1
scaffolds.text: Use the vertical form of Newton's second law, ΣFᵧ = maᵧ. The mass is positive. First infer the acceleration sign from the change in signed velocity, then decide the force direction yourself.

reasoning: The lift moves downward, but its downward speed decreases. Velocity is therefore becoming less negative on an upward-positive axis.
A later velocity minus an earlier velocity is positive, so the acceleration points upward.
By Newton's second law, ΣFᵧ = maᵧ. Because mass is positive, net force is upward.
teacher.check: If the downward speed were constant instead, acceleration and net force would both be zero. Moving down alone does not determine force direction.

feedback.A: This is the intended net-force direction. Compare your written justification with the signed-velocity reasoning below.
feedback.B: This identifies the direction of travel, not necessarily the direction of acceleration. Compare two velocity values.
feedback.C: A steady slowing is still a change in velocity. Zero net force would mean constant velocity.
feedback.D: Mass affects magnitude, but a positive mass does not obscure the direction when acceleration direction is known.

items.stem: Two small robots pull against the ends of the same taut strap. Robot A pulls the strap left with 40 N. Which two forces make a Newton-third-law pair at A's connection to the strap?

options.A: A pulls the strap left with 40 N; gravity pulls A down.
options.B: A pulls the strap left with 40 N; the strap pulls B at its other end.
options.C: A pulls the strap left with 40 N; the strap pulls A right with 40 N.
options.D: The strap pulls A right with 40 N; gravity pulls A down.

changes: Source keyed A is rewritten for explicit equal magnitude and opposite direction and moved to displayed C; correct interaction remains A-on-strap / strap-on-A, 40 N left/right.

Source B: A-on-strap and B-on-strap rewritten as two separate interaction partners at different strap ends (display B: A-on-strap / strap-on-B), not a same-contact reciprocal pair; added B-contact description from stated robot–strap setup, but no B force magnitude or equilibrium assumed.
Source C: A-on-strap and A's weight changed to A-on-strap and gravity-on-A with explicit A's 40 N left on strap; moved to displayed A.
Source D: strap-on-A and floor-on-A rewritten as strap-on-A and gravity-on-A so both forces on A are physically unambiguous without presuming robot-floor contact; displayed D.

All display option edits are distinct from the unaltered source; original stem/40 N left condition, figure, authored provenance, source key A and source QRT EXPLAIN-D1 preserved in source-rows.v1.json.

reasoning: At the A–strap contact, A exerts a force on the strap and the strap exerts a force on A.
The paired forces act on different objects, have the same magnitude (40 N), and point in opposite directions.
Two forces on the strap, or two forces on A, are not each other's Newton-third-law interaction pair.

feedback.A: Different interactions: gravity-on-A and A-on-strap are not the reciprocal pair of one contact.
feedback.B: The listed strap-on-B force occurs at the other robot's connection, not at A's connection; identify the recipient at A's specific contact.
feedback.C: At A's contact, these forces are equal/opposite 40 N and act on A and strap respectively; read the written reasoning before comparing with the teacher answer.
feedback.D: Both listed forces act on A, so they are not a third-law pair of each other.

items.adaptation_defect_note: Source keyed A alone stated opposite 40 N reaction with rightward force while all distractors had less magnitude/direction specificity; previous PU1 wrongly omitted 40 N/rightward and exposed a uniquely bare actor/object reversal. This replacement retains scientific pair detail and tests same-contact force owners with comparable actor-action constructions. Semantic cue risk remains for independent review.
